messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Juan Hernandez had always been a man who cherished his independence, but after what happened in 'Nam, everything changed. It started with the smell of diesel fuel and the acrid taste that lingered on his tongue long after he'd left the battlefield. Even now, 40 years later, the mere whiff of diesel or that same bitter taste would send him reeling – dizzy and disoriented, like he was back in the midst of chaos. As a special education teacher, Juan had always prided himself on being able to connect with his students, but after the war, he found himself increasingly avoiding situations that might stir up strong emotions. He'd steer clear of parent-teacher conferences or staff meetings, opting instead for solo projects that allowed him to maintain a safe distance from others. This self-imposed isolation wasn't just about emotional comfort; it was also about survival – in his mind, if he didn't feel like he was in control, he might as well be back in the trenches. When Juan did venture out into public spaces, he'd always make sure to scope out the nearest exit, mentally mapping escape routes before he felt comfortable enough to focus on anything else. This wasn't just about being prepared; it was an instinct honed from years of living with the constant threat of ambush. Loud noises would still startle him – the sound of a car backfiring or a door slamming shut could send his heart racing – and Juan would find himself scanning his surroundings, searching for signs of danger. As time went on, these habits only intensified. Juan became increasingly hypervigilant, always "on" and ready to respond to potential threats that others might not even notice. This perpetual state of high alert made it difficult for him to relax, even in the safety of his own home. And yet, paradoxically, this constant threat monitoring also seemed to trigger more flashbacks – he'd find himself reliving the horrors of war, his mind flooded with images and sounds that he thought he'd long buried. Talking about the event itself was still almost impossible for Juan; even after all these years, the memories remained too raw, too painful. But what really frightened him was the way these memories seemed to be seeping into other areas of his life – how a simple smell or taste could transport him back to that godforsaken place. It was as if the past was slowly closing in on him, and Juan wasn't sure how much longer he could keep it at bay. Lately, Juan's been feeling like he's losing ground – the avoidance behaviors that used to feel like a necessary evil now seem like they're strangling him. His relationships with his students are suffering, and even his own family is starting to notice the changes in him. That's what finally brought Juan to seek help: the realization that if he didn't confront these demons once and for all, he risked losing everything – including himself.
